niyamavidhi
(‘restrictive injunction’)
------------------------------------------
According to the पूर्वमीमाṁसा Darśana—the fifth in the series of Ṣaḍdarśanas or Six Systems of Hindu Philosophy—the वेदस् are full of vidhis (injunctions) and niṣedhas (prohibitions).
One of the various methods of classification of these vidhis is into three groups: apūrvavidhi (injunction of something quite new); नियमविधि (restrictive injunction); and, parisañkhyāvidhi (precluding one by injunction when two alternatives are possible).
For preparing the पुरोडाश (rice-cake), pounded rice is needed. Though unhusked rice can be dehusked by hand using the fingers or by pounding with a pestle, the Śruti restricts it to the second method as a rule. The sentence ‘vrīhīn avahanti’ (‘He pounds the rice’) is the example for a नियमविधि.

niyoga
(‘appointing’)
------------------------------------------
In ancient societies, there seems to have been an inordinate hankering for a son, who could save a person from any calamity in the next world after death, with appropriate obsequial ceremonies performed here.
Both the Ṛgveda (10.40.2) and the Deuteronomy (25.5-10) section of the Old Testament of the Bible refer to the practice of a childless widow marrying the brother of her husband to raise issues.
‘Niyoga’ literally means ‘appointing’. In a more technical sense it means the appointment of a childless wife or a widow to procreate a son from intercourse with an appointed male.
Frequent wars among the क्षत्त्रिय princes and kings, leading to large scale deaths, leaving behind young childless widows, could have been one of the major causes for this practice. Another cause could have been getting a right over the husband’s property since a childless widow had been debarred from it except bare maintenance.
The Mahābhārata is full of instances of नियोग, the most well-known one being the command of सत्यवती (the मोथेर् of व्यास from the sage पराशर) to व्यास to procreate sons in the two widows of her son Vicitravīrya who died prematurely.
Most of the धर्मशास्त्रस् have condemned the practice—which must have existed in very ancient times—though some have permitted it under stringent conditions.
Eight necessary conditions were laid down, almost all of which were rigorous. The most important of them were that the decision had to be taken by the elders of the family and the person had to be the brother of the husband or belonging to his गोत्र and/or प्रवर. The relation would last only till a son is born.
Gradually the practice was frowned upon by one and all, and was included under the list of कलिवर्ज्य items (things to be avoided in the age of कलि).

niyama
(‘that which restrains’)
------------------------------------------
In the most general sense, the word ‘niyama’ means a rule or discipline. This includes things that are ordained or prohibited, especially during the observance of vratas or religious vows.
In the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) it forms the second of the eight steps of योग and comprises these five disciplines: शौच (cleanliness), सन्तोष (contentment), स्वाध्याय (study of scriptures), तपस् (austerity) and īśvarapraṇi-dhāna (devotion to God and dedication of the fruits of work (vide 2.32).
The Haṭhayogapradīpikā (1.17) gives a longer list of disciplines under नियम. They are: तपस् (austerity), सन्तोष (contentment), āstikya (faith in God), दान (giving gifts, charity), īśvarapūjana (worship of God), सिद्धान्त-vākyaśravaṇa (listening to the statements of the scriptures), hrī (modesty), mati (discerning मिन्द्), जप (repetition of mantras) and huta (sacrifice, oblations in duly consecrated fire).
In Sanskrit grammar it refers to a restricting rule as prevailing over a more general rule.
